description_full: SM Prime Holdings, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, operates, maintains, and leases commercial shopping malls in the Philippines and China. It operates in four segments: Mall; Residential; Commercial and Integrated Property Developments; and Hotels and Convention Centers. The company also operates, maintains, and rents shopping spaces, amusement centers, and cinema theaters. In addition, it is involved in the owning, development, and sale of condominium units, and leisure and resorts; development, operations, management, and leasing of office buildings and land; and development and management of hotels and convention centers properties. SM Prime Holdings, Inc. was founded in 1985 and is based in Pasay City, the Philippines. SM Prime Holdings, Inc. operates as a subsidiary of SM Investments Corporation.

financial_summary: SM PRIME HOLDINGS INC is a mid-cap real estate business with a $7.8B market cap on $2.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 7% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically. Gross margins of 82% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $1.2B in free cash flow — roughly 53 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.53× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.5× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 5.5×.

Shareholder yield of 3.2% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 66% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.5× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (1.1) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Interest-rate sensitivity and tenant-credit risk — cap rates and refinancing costs move faster than the 10-year leases can absorb.
Remote work structural vacancy — the post-pandemic shift to hybrid work has permanently impaired demand for urban office space across most markets.
Climate and insurance cost escalation — rising premiums and coverage withdrawals in flood/fire zones are repricing assets that the market once treated as perpetuities.

sect: Its 51% operating margin runs 28pp above the Real Estate median (23%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.55x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.6% of sector revenue and 1.6% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 145 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 36% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 434% and a beta of 0.94, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.54 vs 5y -3.02), so read it loosely.
Trading is thin (about $1K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 29% in the 2020 crash and 39% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 73% below its DCF fair value of $1.00, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 22%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $0.74 to $1.38 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Real Estate peers: P/E 9.1 vs 23.6, EV/EBITDA 4.9 vs 16.3 and P/FCF 6.6 vs 17.8 (sector median).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 15.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 0.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 8.2% annual cash-flow growth, 15pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 7% earns above the cost of capital of 6.9%, but the 0pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.09).
It runs a 82% gross margin and converts 53% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.53x.
ROE of 10% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.3x equity multiplier).
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.5x net debt to EBITDA ($450.2M of cash against $6.7B of debt), with interest covered 5.5x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.09 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.2% over 3 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
own: Insiders own 66.5%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 8%.
It returns 3.2% a year to shareholders (0.3% in buybacks and 3.7% in dividends).

why: DCF is 286% above the other models' median ($0.26)
